{"id": "22:18/q24", "question": "How is mukrim read?", "turns_on": "Whether the rāʾ has kasra or fatḥa and what noun the fatḥa creates.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q24/p1", "position": "The general reading has kasra on rāʾ, mukrim, an active participle.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī rejects another vocalization on authoritative reader agreement."}, {"id": "22:18/q24/p2", "position": "Ibn Abī ʿAblah reads fatḥa, mukram, meaning honor, a place of honor, or a substantivized passive form.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ālūsī report these semantic possibilities; al-Jishumī compares madkhal and munzal. Al-Ṭabarī rejects it as contrary to authoritative readers."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q25", "question": "How is 'whoever God humiliates' parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q25/p1", "position": "Man is a fronted conditional object; the fāʾ introduces its answer.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives this construction."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q26", "question": "What does 'God does what He wills' affirm?", "turns_on": "How broad divine willing is and how it relates to acts, eternal attributes, and human conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q26/p1", "position": "God freely honors and humiliates, rewards and punishes, and His will cannot be opposed.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī cites God's ownership of creation and command and 21:23; al-Biqāʿī says any independent opponent would prevent God's doing whatever He wills. The ʿAlī report tests a disputant with creation, illness, healing and afterlife destination; related versions appear in Ibn Kathīr, al-Biqāʿī and al-Durr. Al-Ālūsī prefers the universal scope over limiting the clause to honor and humiliation."}, {"id": "22:18/q26/p2", "position": "Divine willing honors some with faith and humiliates others with disbelief or punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī connects honor to faith and humiliation to disbelief; al-Qurṭubī says the condemned end in Hell and no one can object; al-Ṭabrisī names favor and vengeance."}, {"id": "22:18/q26/p3", "position": "The verse refutes the claim that God wills things without doing them.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī explicitly identifies a Muʿtazilite doctrine and argues from 'does whatever He wills'."}, {"id": "22:18/q26/p4", "position": "Divine will is an attribute of action inferred from acts or prepared causes, not an eternal attribute distinct from God's essence.", "reasons": "Al-Riḍā's report denies eternal willing and choosing as monotheism; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says human will names knowledgeable agency when action follows, while God's willing says He did or prepared what He knew best. An eternal distinct will would introduce an uncreated co-eternal. He rejects reducing will to knowledge of the best as an empty extra attribute."}, {"id": "22:18/q26/p5", "position": "Will and people's deeds and beliefs together explain decreed felicity or misery.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī gives this explanation; Abū Ḥayyān identifies Muʿtazilite doctrine in it and objects. Bursevī speaks of eternal knowledge of the person's evil choice."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q27", "question": "Why end with 'God does what He wills'?", "turns_on": "Whether the closing assertion is unrestricted or explained through its immediate contrasts.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q27/p1", "position": "It explains irreversible punishment and humiliation and asserts universal power.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says emphatic inna makes it a cause of the preceding parenthetical statements; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it indirectly asserts power. Al-Ālūsī prefers the universal assertion rather than context-limited honor and humiliation."}, {"id": "22:18/q27/p2", "position": "Its context is specifically divine reward and punishment, felicity and misery, or beneficence and vengeance.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī records the three explanatory pairs through Yaḥyā, al-Farrāʾ and his own addition."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q28", "question": "What does the verse establish about divine power and independent interpretation?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse is used as evidence for divine power or for reasoned access to religious meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q28/p1", "position": "God perfectly subjects creation and directs it according to His will.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī makes universal subjection evidence of perfect power."}, {"id": "22:18/q28/p2", "position": "The verse's intended meaning can be reached by examining proof without an Imam.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī rejects the Imāmī position and says reasoning from evidence yields knowledge of religion against claims that such knowledge is necessary or unreasoned."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q29", "question": "What inward lesson is drawn from prostration and humiliation?", "turns_on": "How authors extend the verse's contrast into spiritual states.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q29/p1", "position": "Gnostics worship knowingly while rejecters' very bodies testify to God.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī cites a couplet on every thing bearing a sign of oneness; Bursevī's Taʾwīlāt contrasts chosen gnosis with compelled need."}, {"id": "22:18/q29/p2", "position": "The condemned wear spiritual deprivation; the faithful wear graded piety and intimacy with God.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī contrasts shirk, falsehood and afterlife pitch (23:108) with piety against association, sin, heedlessness and dependence on other than God, then silk or cloaks of love and solitude in the afterlife."}, {"id": "22:18/q29/p3", "position": "The elect adorn Paradise, and the rare person of union has inviolable honor.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says the elect transcend states, stations and created servitude, with an illustrative pearl couplet. Bursevī says annihilation of self is true prostration and cites the sacred report that harming God's friend declares war on Him."}, {"id": "22:18/q29/p4", "position": "Prostration offers greater delight than worldly fortune.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites a devotional couplet and the Futūḥāt's call to witnessing, reflection and joining the obedient group."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q30", "question": "What prostration of recitation is associated with this verse and Sūrat al-Ḥajj?", "turns_on": "How the reports establish practice and the sūra's count.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q30/p1", "position": "This verse is a recognized place for prostration of recitation, and the sūra has two such places.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports juristic consensus for this passage. A report from ʿUqba b. ʿĀmir says the Prophet confirmed two prostrations and urged their practice; ʿUmar performed two at al-Jābiya, and ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ reports fifteen Qurʾanic prostrations including both in this sūra. A mursal Khālid report agrees. Ibn Kathīr treats the reports as mutual corroboration; al-Tirmidhī called Ibn Lahīʿa's chain weak, which Ibn Kathīr disputes because he explicitly claimed hearing. Abū Dāwūd says another connected route is unsound. Kāshifī calls this the sixth Qurʾanic prostration by consensus."}, {"id": "22:18/q30/p2", "position": "The Prophet and Companions prostrated on reciting this verse.", "reasons": "Muqātil reports the event; a dream report through Ibn ʿAbbās describes a tree praying while prostrate and the Prophet repeating its words. A report from Abū Hurayra says Satan weeps when Adam's child prostrates at a prostration verse, recalling his own refusal and Fire."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q31", "question": "How does the verse connect with its immediate context?", "turns_on": "Whether the link centers on the adjacent group contrast, idols, prior sūra, or divine witnessing.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q31/p1", "position": "It continues the contrast between rival groups and explains their judgment through submission, reward, humiliation and punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says it explains the deeds behind the preceding division; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says God witnesses, judges and separates disputants while even refusers remain inwardly subdued. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the dual demonstrative in the next verse points to worshippers of God and polytheists. Iṣlāḥī describes the larger passage's monotheism, Hereafter, cosmic signs, and respective outcomes."}, {"id": "22:18/q31/p2", "position": "It renews proof of God's sole divinity after the helpless beings invoked in 22:12–13.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the intervening material a digression; Iṣlāḥī sees the creatures' submission as an indirect proof of monotheism, exposing the disgrace of worshipping inferior beings."}, {"id": "22:18/q31/p3", "position": "It answers an implied question about God's sovereignty after the prior sūra's account of omnipotence, will and knowledge.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī explicitly links the sūras and asks how God's rule extends across creatures and their states."}, {"id": "22:18/q31/p4", "position": "It may show that God witnesses everything or rebuke doubters of His judgment.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports both functions, adding that evidence should remove the doubt."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q32", "question": "Which other verses illuminate creation's prostration and the humiliation warning?", "turns_on": "Which cited parallels specify the cosmic and moral claims.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q32/p1", "position": "Verses on universal submission, shadows and praise illuminate the same theme.", "reasons": "Commentators cite 13:15, 16:48–49, 17:44, 21:79, 24:41, 34:10 and 55:6; Iṣlāḥī says 24:41 treats visible obedience and inward praise, while Asad directs readers to 13:15 and 16:48–49. Study Quran also cites 13:13."}, {"id": "22:18/q32/p2", "position": "The impossibility of reversing God's disgrace parallels divine guidance and help passages.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 18:17 and 3:160; Iṣlāḥī cites 4:115 for God's leaving a person to chosen conduct after proof."}]}

{"id": "22:18/q34", "question": "How does implied meaning or concision help explain this verse's unstated halves?", "turns_on": "Whether brevity works through inferred opposites or a change of sense in an implied word.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q34/p1", "position": "Its compact contrast implies the omitted reward and refusal.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says prostration in the first group implies its absence in the second, and punishment in the second implies reward for the first. Al-Burhān calls concise expression eloquent when shorter than the usual amount for its meaning; it cites the Prophet's gift of comprehensive concise speech and examples 7:199 and 6:82. Al-Rummānī says valid implication is economical expression and divine speech conveys every sound implication of its wording."}, {"id": "22:18/q34/p2", "position": "A supplied governor with another sense approaches istikhdām.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī compares a repeated unexpressed word in another sense to a pronoun recalling a word in a changed sense."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q35", "question": "What grammar supports or limits omission around kathīr?", "turns_on": "Whether nominative resumption, accusative government, or coordination best handles the two many clauses.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q35/p1", "position": "A fronted nominative may be resumed by a later pronoun, supporting independent predication.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites time and place nouns with a later pronoun; al-Farrāʾ says ḥaqqa ʿalayhi resumes the second kathīr. Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats it as a detached subject."}, {"id": "22:18/q35/p2", "position": "An accusative may be governed as an adverb or by an understood verb; it is the more common form in Sībawayh's analogous constructions.", "reasons": "Sībawayh accepts several accusative analyses and prefers the recognized accusative; al-Farrāʾ permits accusative kathīran, and al-Qurṭubī supplies an omitted verb meaning God humbled many."}, {"id": "22:18/q35/p3", "position": "Omitting a resumptive pronoun is possible in poetry but weak in prose.", "reasons": "Sībawayh cites Abū al-Najm's object omission, Imruʾ al-Qays's 'a garment I wore', al-Namir's day/month expressions, Jarīr's adjectival clause and al-Ḥārith's omitted object. He says an adjective completes its noun and cannot become an independent clause whose missing pronoun is replaced with accusative."}, {"id": "22:18/q35/p4", "position": "Coordination brings a second noun under the same governor, while a circumstantial wāw opens a separate proposition.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī explains the shared governor for coordination, and distinguishes the wāw of a resumed circumstance from an integrated predicate by comparing 'Zayd came while he was hurrying' with 'Zayd came hurrying'."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q36", "question": "How are particle clauses and their implied relations analyzed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q36/p1", "position": "Particles operate on whole predications, and causal or emphatic clauses may stand independently.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says inna after illā can begin independently if ungoverned, with lām marking initial position as in 25:20; in an anger example illā anna has the sense 'only because'. His oath examples include mā inna. Al-Jurjānī says negation, interrogation and condition govern an attributed action, compares lā rajula, kaʾanna, law and lawlā, and says particle plus noun or verb is incomplete except vocative with implied verb. Ibn ʿĀshūr says emphatic inna here conveys causal explanation."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q37", "question": "What morphology or Arabic poetry is cited in discussing this verse?", "turns_on": "The difference between a morphological analysis and poetic evidence for lexical usage.", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q37/p1", "position": "Kathīr is an adjective on the faʿīl pattern with an added yāʾ.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives the pattern for nouns and adjectives; kathīr is his verse example."}, {"id": "22:18/q37/p2", "position": "Poetry is a witness to difficult Arabic meanings, not a source from which the Qurʾān is derived.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbārī answers critics using the Qurʾān's Arabic character; Ibn ʿAbbās calls poetry the Arabs' register, and Abū ʿUbayd says his poetic citations served as evidence. Al-Suyūṭī collected the questions of Nāfiʿ b. al-Azraq; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports the same method and witnesses."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q38", "question": "What is known about the transmitted Ibn ʿAbbās poetry questions cited for rare words?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q38/p1", "position": "The recensions differ, and their manuscript relationships can be traced.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the Cairo K and Ṭ copies likely descend from a fourth-century manuscript; Ṭ may derive from K, with two omitted disruptive passages and no recorded copyist/date. The opening places Ibn ʿAbbās at the Kaʿba challenged by Nāfiʿ and Najda; only al-Mubarrad has the ʿUmar b. Abī Rabīʿa episode. The Ẓāhiriyya manuscript and al-Ṭabarānī share 31 questions through ʿUthmān al-Ḥarrānī; K and Ṭ align with abridged al-Itqān through Ibn al-Ṭastī. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ names the manuscript, al-Haythamī and source works as editorial comparanda."}]}
{"id": "22:18/q39", "question": "What illustrative simile analysis accompanies discussion of expression?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:18/q39/p1", "position": "Unusual composite likenesses require attention to coordinated motion and appearance.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī explains yiqtāʿuhā as a calf climbing onto its kneeling mother and likens its irregular limbs to a person climbing a ladder. He says novel composite configurations are rarer than wheel, mill or arrow motions, and analyzes a shaking mirror's light moving inward from the rim."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q01", "question": "Who were the people expelled from their homes?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse describes the emigrants generally, Muhammad with his companions, or extends to his family.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q01/p1", "position": "Believers expelled by Quraysh from Mecca, especially the Emigrants.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Baydawi name Mecca and Quraysh; Razi uses 22:41 to distinguish the emigrants from the Helpers. Al-Tabataba'i says the whole community is described by some members' ordeal."}, {"id": "22:40/q01/p2", "position": "Muhammad and his companions specifically.", "reasons": "Sa'id ibn Jubayr relates the alarm at the Prophet's departure; Ibn Abbas names the Prophet and companions and their move to Medina."}, {"id": "22:40/q01/p3", "position": "The emigrants, with the Prophet's family also included by application.", "reasons": "Abu Ja'far says the family of Muhammad too were expelled and intimidated."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q02", "question": "How were the believers driven out, and where did they go?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in destination and in whether expulsion means direct removal or persecution that forced departure.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q02/p1", "position": "Quraysh tortured, threatened, and harassed believers until they left Mecca for Medina.", "reasons": "Muqatil and Tabari describe torture and threats; Ibn al-Arabi says some were tempted from faith. Tabataba'i says compelled departure, not physical deportation."}, {"id": "22:40/q02/p2", "position": "Some fled to Abyssinia, others to Medina, and some endured in Mecca.", "reasons": "Tabrisi treats Medina as implying a Medinan revelation and Abyssinia as implying a Meccan one; Biqa'i also names the mountain valley."}, {"id": "22:40/q02/p3", "position": "Specific Meccan emigrants were prevented from migrating to Medina.", "reasons": "Mujahid says fighting was permitted against the unbelievers who blocked their migration."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q03", "question": "How does 'those expelled' attach grammatically to the previous verse?", "turns_on": "The relative may continue an earlier relative in the genitive or stand in the nominative or accusative by ellipsis.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q03/p1", "position": "It is genitive, qualifying or replacing the preceding relative expression.", "reasons": "Tabari says the second relative resumes those permitted to fight; Ibn Ashur ties it to 22:39. Kashshaf calls the genitive most apparent."}, {"id": "22:40/q03/p2", "position": "It is accusative with an implied 'I mean' or as praise.", "reasons": "Tabrisi and Samin give an omitted verb of specification or praise."}, {"id": "22:40/q03/p3", "position": "It is nominative with an implied subject such as 'they'.", "reasons": "The construction begins a nominal clause with an understood subject."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q04", "question": "How is the expulsion attributed to Quraysh if believers left under pressure?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q04/p1", "position": "A forced departure is attributed to the coercer, assigning blame to Quraysh.", "reasons": "Qurtubi compares 9:40, 'when the unbelievers expelled him'; Tabataba'i details persecution forcing departure."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q05", "question": "What spiritual failings can betray the way of those defended by God?", "turns_on": "Qushayri distinguishes motives by spiritual station.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q05/p1", "position": "Ascetics, worshippers, gnostics, lovers and unifiers each risk betrayal at their own station.", "reasons": "Qushayri names seeking afterlife compensation, falling back on concessi

Biqa'i says sincere devotion attracts plots and harm."}, {"id": "22:40/q05/p2", "position": "God protects the common through the elect as a lasting divine custom.", "reasons": "Qushayri says He pardons lesser people for the honor of the great."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q06", "question": "What does diyār denote and how is dār derived?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q06/p1", "position": "It is their dwellings, homes, or country; dār denotes an enclosed circuit.", "reasons": "Bursevi says the plural can denote countries because inhabitants move within them; al-Raghib derives dār from a wall's circuit."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q07", "question": "May houses in Mecca be sold or leased?", "turns_on": "Whether residents own their houses despite pilgrimage access.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q07/p1", "position": "Sale and lease are permissible.", "reasons": "Baghawi prefers this: the verse calls the homes theirs; the Prophet called Abu Sufyan's house his, and Umar bought a Meccan house for a prison for four thousand dirhams. Tawus, Amr ibn Dinar, and al-Shafi'i allow sale."}, {"id": "22:40/q07/p2", "position": "Sale and lease are impermissible because pilgrims have common access.", "reasons": "Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit says pilgrims had equal entitlement to houses; Umar forbade closing doors during pilgrimage."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q08", "question": "What makes the expulsion 'without right'?", "turns_on": "The sources distinguish the absence of a lawful offense from the inherent right to remain in one's homeland.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q08/p1", "position": "They committed no wrong; their sole alleged offense was affirming God's oneness.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan says they shed no blood, stole no property, and severed no kinship, citing 85:8; Ibn Kathir cites 60:1 and 85:8; Razi cites 5:59. Ibn Ashur says a declaration of faith harms no one. Al-Jubba'i says no action merited exile; Ibn Ashur notes the religious cause."}, {"id": "22:40/q08/p2", "position": "People have a natural right to live in their homeland unless a valid law or custom warrants exile.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur traces the right to settlement or conquest; legitimate banishment punishes wrongdoing, and Zuhayr's verse illustrates old customary grounds."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q09", "question": "How does 'without right' work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Circumstantial qualification versus an omitted verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q09/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial phrase describing the exiles' unjust state.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says no valid ground existed for imposing removal."}, {"id": "22:40/q09/p2", "position": "It qualifies an omitted cognate verbal noun: an unjust expulsion.", "reasons": "Tabrisi supplies an understood 'expulsion'."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q10", "question": "How is the exception 'except that they say' parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether the construction is disconnected, connected to ḥaqq, or uses an adjectival 'other than'; Abu Hayyan disputes the proposed apposition.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q10/p1", "position": "It is connected to the supposed 'right' or cause, grammatically genitive through bāʾ or appositive to ḥaqq.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and Zajjaj allow understood bāʾ; Wahidi cites 92:20, al-Mubarrad's connected pretext, and al-Nabigha's ironic sword nicks. Alusi rejects objections to the apposition."}, {"id": "22:40/q10/p2", "position": "It is a disconnected accusative exception, with illā meaning 'but' or 'because'.", "reasons": "Sibawayh gives Qur'anic parallels 11:43, 10:98, 11:116 and poets; Abu Hayyan says a positive governor cannot reach the exception and Arabs agree on accusative here. Tabataba'i prefers the contrast. Nahhas transmits Sibawayh's non-connected accusative and Abu Hayyan's objection. Qurtubi transmits Farra and Zajjaj's genitive cause."}, {"id": "22:40/q10/p3", "position": "Illā is an adjective meaning 'other than' (siwā) of ḥaqq.", "reasons": "Alusi offers this alternative; Samin distinguishes it from the rejected apposition."}, {"id": "22:40/q10/p4", "position": "The exception is elliptic: 'except that they say the truth'.", "reasons": "Abu Ubayda supplies the omitted truth."}, {"id": "22:40/q10/p5", "position": "It is appositive to ghayr, implying they were only maintained in their homes by profession.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this parse but calls it weak."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q11", "question": "Why present their confession as an exception to wrongdoing?", "turns_on": "The paradox treats a virtue as a supposed fault.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q11/p1", "position": "The ironic exception intensifies innocence and praises them by feigning blame.", "reasons": "Wahidi, Baydawi, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur invoke al-Nabigha's 'only fault' of battle-nicked swords; Kashshaf, Nasafi and Razi compare 5:59. Islahi says Quraysh treated the greatest truth as the greatest sin."}, {"id": "22:40/q11/p2", "position": "It states the sole actual cause of persecution: affirmation of one God.", "reasons": "Qatada says monotheism distressed Satan and his troops; Tabataba'i says polytheists perversely treated truth as grounds for eviction."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q12", "question": "What did Quraysh understand by the confession?", "turns_on": "Whether they viewed it as a harmless private belief or understood its social force.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q12/p1", "position": "They recognized its far-reaching implications and opposed it.", "reasons": "Islahi says their opposition to the greatest truth was deliberate."}, {"id": "22:40/q12/p2", "position": "They harassed Muslims for an innocuous belief.", "reasons": "Some interpreters see profession of one God as no offense."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q13", "question": "How does 'were it not for' work here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q13/p1", "position": "Lawlā introduces a counterfactual: destruction does not occur because God's defense does occur.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur explains the consequent is withheld by the existence of the condition."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q14", "question": "How is 'God's repelling' read and formed?", "turns_on": "Whether the verbal noun is Form I dafʿ or difāʿ with alif and how it relates to the corresponding verb.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q14/p1", "position": "Difāʿ with alif is read with yudāfiʿ and suggests mutual or sustained defense.", "reasons": "Nafi, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub are reported among its readers. Abu Ali compares qitāl from qātala; Jishumi calls difāʿ reciprocal."}, {"id": "22:40/q14/p2", "position": "Dafʿ without alif is read, including with yadfaʿ without alif.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr use the simple form; Asim is reported with dafʿ. Qiraat-ER says Form I may indicate one act. {"id": "22:40/q18", "question": "What legal duty follows from God's protecting worship?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse directly establishes defensive fighting, religious liberty, and wider moral duties.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q18/p1", "position": "Believers may fight defensively to protect worship and freedom of religion.", "reasons": "Qurtubi says earlier communities also used jihad; Asad calls defense of religious freedom a foremost reason for arms, citing 2:193 and 2:251; Kuran Yolu cites passages on defensive preparations."}, {"id": "22:40/q18/p2", "position": "The verse also indicates a duty to command right and forbid wrong.", "reasons": "Jishumi infers the obligation; Uthman's report links 22:40–41 to later command of right."}]}
{"id": "22:40/q19", "question": "What inward meaning is given to the repelling and the worship places?", "turns_on": "The inward readings assign the conflict to faculties, the ego and spiritual aspiration.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q19/p1", "position": "Divine help lets hearts resist the ego so sacred law, spiritual manners, reality and remembrance endure.", "reasons": "Qushayri says promptings corrupt hearts and God defeats them by turning and unveiling; Bursevi describes mosques of the heart."}, {"id": "22:40/q19/p2", "position": "God counters psychic forces through spirit and intellect; the four sites mark secret, heart, breast, and spirit.", "reasons": "Qashani sets desire against anger, spirit against psyche and intellect against fancy; remembrance culminates in divine character and annihilation."}, {"id": "22:40/q19/p3", "position": "The saints may seem humiliated, yet God avenges or later empowers them.", "reasons": "Qushayri cites 27:52 and says truth outlasts falsehood."}, {"id": "22:40/q19/p4", "position": "God overcomes self-exalting claims of independent existence with His light.", "reasons": "Qashani applies divine victory inwardly."}]}

{"id": "22:40/q42", "question": "What does naṣr mean?", "turns_on": "Help versus revenge, rain, or coming to a place in broader Arabic usage.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q42/p1", "position": "Here it means giving help to God's cause.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi cites 59:12 and 47:7."}, {"id": "22:40/q42/p2", "position": "In other uses naṣr may mean rain or coming to a place, while intiṣār can mean revenge.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi quotes a poem using unṣurī for visiting a land."}]}

{"id": "22:40/q46", "question": "What do 'strong' and 'mighty' affirm of God?", "turns_on": "Distinct glosses of might emphasize invincibility, exaltation, or retribution.", "positions": [{"id": "22:40/q46/p1", "position": "He has unrestricted power to aid believers and cannot be overcome or resisted.", "reasons": "Tabari contrasts idols' inability to create or protect a fly (22:73); Ibn Kathir invokes creation and decree; Ibn Ashur distinguishes strength as power and might as invulnerability."}, {"id": "22:40/q46/p2", "position": "Mighty can stress vengeance against enemies.", "reasons": "Muqatil's gloss and Yahya ibn Sallam's account emphasize retribution."}, {"id": "22:40/q46/p3", "position": "Mighty can mean exalted and noble.", "reasons": "Qurtubi transmits Zajjaj's gloss."}]}
